analysis.one_liner: Lifts bans on offshore oil and gas drilling across the entire Outer Continental Shelf.
analysis.headline: The bill never left committee: it was introduced in September 2005, sent to a House subcommittee, and died when the 109th Congress ended in January 2007 without ever getting a vote.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would wipe out every federal law that blocks spending money on oil and gas leasing in federal offshore waters, cancel existing presidential withdrawals protecting areas from drilling, and force the Interior Department to hold a lease sale in the Eastern Gulf of Mexico within 180 days. In short, it would open the entire Outer Continental Shelf to oil and gas companies. It never advanced past a subcommittee.
analysis.who_benefits: Oil and gas companies, which would gain access to lease and drill on vast areas of federal offshore waters currently closed by spending bans and presidential withdrawals, including a mandated lease sale in the Eastern Gulf of Mexico.

how_it_helps.text: It declares that all federal laws prohibiting spending on offshore oil and gas leasing and preleasing 'shall have no force or effect,' removing the annual bans that kept most of the Outer Continental Shelf closed to drilling. [S3]
It revokes all existing presidential withdrawals under the Outer Continental Shelf Lands Act, ending protections that presidents had placed on offshore areas. [S2][S3]

It directs the Interior Secretary to conduct a lease sale on all submerged lands of the Eastern Gulf of Mexico depicted in a 2001 lease-sale document but not already leased, within 180 days of enactment. [S2][S3]

Supporters could argue that opening these areas would expand domestic oil and gas supply at a time when energy prices were a leading concern; the record does not include committee findings on this, so the size of any supply effect is not established by the sources. [S1]

analysis.who_pays: Coastal communities and the public bear the environmental risk: lifting the bans and presidential withdrawals would expose protected offshore areas to drilling, with spill and ecosystem risks falling on coastlines, fisheries, and tourism economies rather than on the leasing companies.

drawbacks.text: Nullifying the offshore leasing bans and revoking presidential withdrawals would open areas long protected from drilling, placing spill and environmental risk on coastal states, fisheries, and tourism economies that had no way to opt out. [S2][S3]

The bill would force a lease sale in the Eastern Gulf of Mexico on 180 days' notice, removing the discretion that both Congress and presidents had used to keep that area off the auction block. [S2][S3]

An honest supporter would have to acknowledge that leasing moratoria exist in large part because coastal states objected to drilling off their shores, and this bill overrides those objections without offering coastal states anything in return. [S2]

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill's benefit — more domestic drilling acreage for energy producers — is real but speculative in size, and the sources contain no analysis of how much oil and gas it would actually yield. Its costs are concentrated and concrete: coastal environments, fishing grounds, and tourism economies would absorb the spill risk of drilling in previously protected waters. On the record provided, the transfer runs clearly toward the industry and the risk toward the public.

outcome.mechanism: It sat in the House Natural Resources Committee and then its Energy and Mineral Resources Subcommittee for the rest of the Congress and expired without a hearing, a markup, or any floor vote.

narrative.text: Rep. Ted Poe introduced the bill on September 15, 2005, and it was referred the same day to the House Committee on Resources. [S1][S5]
Six days later, on September 21, 2005, it was sent to the Subcommittee on Energy and Mineral Resources, where committee work happens before a bill can move to the full House. [S5]
The sponsor gave introductory remarks on the measure twice in October 2005, but no further legislative action was ever recorded. [S5]
Eleven Republicans cosponsored the bill; no Democrat did. [S4]
The bill never received a vote in committee or on the House floor and died when the 109th Congress ended on January 3, 2007. [S1][S5]

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Because the bill died without action, the existing offshore leasing bans and presidential withdrawals stayed in force, and coastal communities, fishing and tourism interests, and the ocean areas they depend on were spared the drilling exposure the bill would have created. Oil and gas companies gained nothing from this bill, though the closed areas remained closed only by the same laws the bill targeted.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Coastal communities and the protected offshore areas

against.what_they_did: Received the referral, sent it to the Energy and Mineral Resources Subcommittee, and took no further action — no hearing, no markup, no vote — for the rest of the Congress.

sides.party_line_note: All 12 sponsors and cosponsors were Republicans; there is no record of any Democratic support, and the bill never reached a vote where partisan positions would have been recorded.

industries.note: The bill hands the industry leasing access to the entire Outer Continental Shelf, including a mandatory Eastern Gulf of Mexico sale, by nullifying the spending bans and presidential withdrawals that keep those waters closed. The industry's gain comes at the expense of coastal environmental protections ordinary people rely on.

Opening previously withdrawn offshore areas to drilling would put spill risk on the coastlines, fisheries, and beach economies these industries depend on; their interest ran with the public's in keeping the bans in place.
